item.title: Parisian women defied trouser ban in 19th century
item.description: In 1800, wearing trousers was banned for women in Paris, intended to keep women out of political life. Yet throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, many Parisian women continued to break or circumvent this law, dressing and even living as men. Writer George Sand wore men's clothing for practical reasons: it gave her access to places reserved for men,...

item.title: Botero's round figures breathe new life into classical masterpieces
item.description: Colombian artist Fernando Botero reimagined famous European artworks, such as the Mona Lisa, in his distinctive rounded style, known as 'Boterismo'. This style emerged in 1956 when he accidentally painted a hole that was too small in a mandoline, causing the instrument to appear to 'explode' in form and volume. item.title: Gabriela Ponce Santizo: 19 years of nature conservation in Guatemala
item.description: Gabriela Ponce Santizo, a Guatemalan biologist, has been active in nature conservation for 19 years and is now Country Director of the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) in Guatemala. item.title: Ocean protector Stacy Jupiter fights breast cancer
item.description: Dr. Stacy Jupiter, who coordinates global ocean conservation for the Wildlife Conservation Society, received an unexpected breast cancer diagnosis in September 2025 while on vacation in Florida. There was no visible tumor in her breast, but the cancer had already spread to her lymph nodes. She returned to Boston for treatment, where she underwent a clinical trial, surgery, chemotherapy and...

item.title: NASA SpaceX mission delivers experiments and solar panels to ISS
item.description: NASA's latest SpaceX cargo resupply mission has successfully launched toward the International Space Station (ISS). The flight carries thousands of pounds of supplies, scientific equipment, and new technology to the station. This cargo is intended to support research in Earth orbit. In addition to crew necessities, the mission also includes solar panels for the ISS.

item.title: NASA invites companies to develop next-generation space stations
item.description: On October 9, 2026, NASA published a final request for proposals inviting American companies to develop the next generation of commercial space stations. item.description: Two weeks after its launch, the European Copernicus satellite Sentinel-3C has transmitted its first images and measurements to Earth. item.title: Europe launches 13 new hubs for open research data
item.description: Researchers in Europe are gaining easier access to research data and digital services thanks to the launch of the first 13 hubs within the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC) Federation. These so-called EOSC Nodes connect research resources from different organizations and help scientists collaborate across borders and disciplines. item.description: NASA and the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) signed a new cooperation agreement in early October during the Science: A Golden Age Summit in Washington to accelerate nuclear energy and nuclear propulsion for space missions. item.description: Researchers at the University of California, San Francisco have demonstrated for the first time in humans that the psychedelic psilocybin can reduce inflammation markers. In a small pilot study with 12 participants with Parkinson's disease, five inflammatory signaling molecules were measured in the blood before and after two psilocybin sessions. item.title: Crows make decisions twice as fast as humans
item.description: New research published in the journal Science shows that crows convert visual information into decisions at remarkable speed — twice as fast as humans and primates. Researcher Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen trained crows to perform a classic test also used in humans and apes: recognizing the direction of moving dots on a screen. item.title: Rare jaguar filmed near Guatemala-Honduras border
item.description: In June, camera traps captured a male jaguar in Guatemala's forest areas, close to the border with Honduras. Conservation organization Panthera calls the footage, which occurs only once every ten years, a milestone for the jaguar species threatened in Guatemala. item.description: At the Waterfowl Sanctuary in Godmanchester, England, Graham Porter received a call from an angler whose fishing line had hooked a young swan. The man had tried to free the bird himself, but was attacked by the protective father swan. item.title: HART Rescue saves feral cats as farm cats
item.description: In 2015, Jennifer Cabral and Deb Mathews founded HART Rescue in Crossville, Tennessee. Instead of euthanizing feral, semi-feral or unsocialized cats, the organization places them as working farm cats with local farmers. To date, 634 cats have been rehomed this way. item.title: Threatened leopard shark spotted for first time in Samoan waters
item.description: Scientists from National Geographic Pristine Seas have filmed a leopard shark, also known as a zebra shark, in Samoan waters for the first time. The footage was captured using a Baited Remote Underwater Video (BRUV), a camera system placed on the seafloor without divers to document marine life. item.title: Sloth bear Vasi receives first-ever bear prosthetic
item.description: Vasikaran, a sloth bear from India nicknamed Vasi, lost his left hind leg in 2019 after it became trapped in a snare. The organization Wildlife SOS rescued him, but veterinarians had to amputate the limb. item.title: Floating wetlands bring nature back to Bristol Harbour
item.description: Climate activists and conservation charity WWT have created floating wetlands along the concrete quays of Bristol Harbour. The platforms, measuring 100 and 16 square metres, are made entirely from recycled, recyclable and biodegradable materials, such as old water pipes and coconut fibres. More than 20 native plants have been planted on a layer of floating clay pellets. Above water, a...

item.description: Mussels, oysters, cockles and scallops filter water and improve water quality, while mussel farms increase biodiversity in surrounding areas. item.description: A new study shows that working from home brings colleagues closer together rather than driving them apart. item.title: Three Michigan tribes aim to restore vanished Arctic grayling
item.description: In Michigan, three Native American tribes are working together with the state to bring back the Arctic grayling, a fish that disappeared from the region in the 1930s due to logging, overfishing, and competition from non-native species. item.title: Nurses secure first county-level paid parental leave in the US
item.description: Nurses at UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital in Pittsburgh, including neonatal nurse Jean Stone, joined forces with working parents, advocates and elected officials to form a coalition for paid parental leave. item.title: Halloween skeletons raise 2 million dollars for St. Jude
item.description: More than 600 American households are participating in Skeletons for St. Jude, a fundraising initiative that began when Jeff Robertson from Holly Springs, North Carolina shared his Halloween decoration with a child battling cancer in 2020. item.title: Sea otters Juno, Lincoln and Uni Sushi play basketball with pumpkins
item.description: The Oregon Zoo shared a video on October 24 of three rescued sea otters swimming, splashing and tossing pumpkins into basketball hoops. The otters Juno, Lincoln and Uni Sushi regularly play basketball in their Steller Cove habitat, with the rubber ball replaced by mini pumpkins around Halloween. item.title: 15-year-old develops QR code with medical emergency information
item.description: After a classmate collapsed at school and no one knew her medical details, 15-year-old Aanya Mansani from Texas developed the platform Emergen. Via a QR code on an ID badge, backpack or phone case, for example, bystanders can see essential information directly without an app or login, such as allergies, medications, conditions and trusted contacts. item.description: Off the coast of Cornwall, researchers tested two clever inventions to protect seabirds from drowning in fishing nets: buoys with large, rotating eyes and kites shaped like birds of prey.
